home.title: A status light for Claude Code and other coding agents.
home.subtitle: Green while it's working, yellow when it's waiting on you, red when it's idle.
home.stripAriaLabel: Simulated status light cycling through idle, working, waiting, and compacting states

whyItExists.heading: No terminal to check, no app to open.
whyItExists.body: A terminal or dashboard only tells you something if you're looking at it. This doesn't. It sits on your desk and shows the same thing whether you're at your keyboard or not.

whatItIs.heading: Ten LEDs. A USB-C board. A small CLI.
whatItIs.body: Ten addressable LEDs behind a diffuser, wired to a USB-C dev board, driven by a small Python CLI (a program you run by typing a command, not something with a window or icon). Claude Code hooks send state changes to the CLI, which updates the light: green while it's working, yellow when it's waiting on you, red when it's idle.

waiting.label: Waiting
waiting.description: It needs you: a permission or an answer.

openHardware.heading: Open hardware, honestly a hobby project.
openHardware.body: MIT-licensed: schematics, firmware, and CLI all included. Linux and Windows supported today. Not a commercial product, not for sale. Built because a physical light is more fun to build, and more useful to have, than another terminal tab.

hero.title: Ten LEDs, one wire, no dashboard.
hero.subtitle: How Agent Andon Light turns hook events into light: the board, the protocol, and the firmware (the program that runs directly on the chip).

overview.heading: What's actually on the desk
overview.body: A small circuit board (a Waveshare RP2040-Zero), hand-soldered onto a custom PCB, driving 10 addressable WS2812B LEDs behind a 3D-printed diffuser. One USB-C cable carries both power and the serial connection back to your machine. No separate power supply, no wireless pairing, nothing to configure beyond installing the CLI (the command-line program that talks to the board).
overview.diagramAriaLabel: Diagram of the board: an RP2040-Zero, a USB-C connector, and a row of 10 addressable LEDs split into a status pixel plus green, yellow, and red sections

howItWorks.heading: One character, one color
howItWorks.body: The host CLI talks to the firmware over USB serial with about the simplest protocol that could work: a single ASCII character plus a newline. No JSON, no handshake.

reliability.heading: Built to be trusted while you're not looking
reliability.body: A 30-minute watchdog runs on the firmware itself. If it stops hearing from the host, the red section switches from solid to a slow breathing pulse instead of freezing on a stale color. A status light you walk away from has to fail visibly, not silently.

hooks.heading: Wired straight into Claude Code
hooks.body: Claude Code hooks call the CLI directly, one event at a time, waiting for each call to finish before moving to the next. That's what keeps the light showing the true order of events, even during a turn with a lot of tool calls back to back.

openSource.heading: Nothing hidden
openSource.body: MIT-licensed, start to finish: schematics, firmware, host CLI, and the hook config it installs. The full parts list (bill of materials) and build guide are in the docs if you want to build your own.

product.disclaimer: Windows installer is unsigned. Windows shows a warning before you run it, every time, until it gets signed. macOS isn't tested and isn't officially supported. Built and maintained by one person, not a company. Issues and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.
